To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) lesbian couples who specialize in market versus household production have significantly different levels of labor force participation, and that (b) the labor supply gap by lesbian couple type is substantially reduced when we control for children.

(1) the sexual orientation gap is larger between primary earners, than secondary earners, (2) controlling for children significantly decreases differences in the extensive margin of labor supply between primary earners, but not secondary earners, and (3) controlling for children decreases differences between primary earners in both the extensive margin and the intensive margin of labor supply, but only decreases the intensive margin of work for secondary earners.

(1) the sexual orientation gap is larger for lesbian primary than lesbian secondary earners, (2) the effect of children is understated when household specialization is not taken into consideration, (3) the effect of controlling children is larger for secondary than primary earners, and (4) the effect of the children variable is not uniform across conditional annual hours.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of specialization in household production in the labor market decisions of women in lesbian couples, and the implications of such specialization for the sexual orientation gap.
the role that the division of labor within the household plays in explaining the sexual orientation gap.
the role of the household division of production in explaining labor supply differences between married women (the reference group) and partnered lesbian women (the comparison group).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sexual orientation gap is not primarily due to children but rather to the fact that lesbian secondary earners are more likely to be out of the labor force than married women.
children play a role in explaining labor supply differences between lesbian and married women, but the role is more complicated than is often suggested in the literature.
lesbian couples with children do not have a significantly different labor supply pattern than married couples with children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the role of the household division of production and the presence of children in explaining differences in female labor supply by sexual orientation has been greatly underestimated.

the sexual orientation gap is larger between primary earners than between secondary earners, and that the role of childbearing in explaining differences between married and lesbian women is greatly understated when household specialization is not accounted for.
lesbian secondary earners are more similar to married women than lesbian primary earners are.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the household division of production labor is an important determinant of the sexual orientation gap.
the household division of production is important to consider when studying the sexual orientation gap.
the labor supply gap between partnered lesbian women and married women is substantially larger for secondary earners than for primary earners.
